title: Ufo Eric-Atuanya On the Game-Changing Mission of the Okavango Circle
excerpt: In this exclusive interview, Okavango Circle Co-Chair Ufo Eric-Atuanya discusses the initiative’s bold ambitions beyond minerals and investment pledges, with a focus on building industries, advancing technology and securing a greater African stake in the global economy. By Ajong Mbapndah L*
content:
In this exclusive interview, Okavango Circle Co-Chair Ufo Eric-Atuanya discusses the initiative’s bold ambitions beyond minerals and investment pledges, with a focus on building industries, advancing technology and securing a greater African stake in the global economy.

By Ajong Mbapndah L*

Africa has no shortage of natural wealth, investment opportunities or ambitious ideas. Turning these advantages into thriving industries and lasting prosperity, however, remains a formidable challenge. For Ufo Eric-Atuanya, a seasoned international finance and business development executive with more than three decades of experience, the answer lies in moving beyond promises to bankable projects, productive enterprises and partnerships that deliver results.

As Founder and Co-Chair of the Okavango Circle Steering Committee, Eric-Atuanya is bringing that philosophy to an initiative with far-reaching international ambitions. Through Rimsom Global, the strategic finance and transaction development platform he leads, he has worked across infrastructure, energy, manufacturing, transportation and emerging technologies, connecting investment opportunities with capital and commercial expertise. His experience has convinced him that Africa’s economic transformation requires more than investment pledges; it demands effective institutions, sound financing and the capacity to turn opportunities into functioning businesses.

Inspired in part by Botswana President Duma Boko’s challenge for Africa to capture greater value from its natural resources, the Okavango Circle made its international debut during UNGA 81 in New York. Working alongside fellow Co-Chairs Jude Kearney and Ijeoma D. Agboti-Obatoyinbo, Eric-Atuanya is helping develop a platform connecting African priorities with global investment, technology and economic decision-making. The initiative has outlined preliminary ambitions to develop 10 to 15 investment-ready projects and help at least five reach financial close within five years, subject to validation.

For Eric-Atuanya, whose career has also been shaped by a commitment to stronger Africa–United States commercial relations, the ultimate objective is to give Africa a greater stake in the industries and technologies shaping tomorrow’s economy. “Africa must not only participate in the global economic future; it must help architect it,” he argues.

In this exclusive interview, Eric-Atuanya discusses the origins of the Okavango Circle, President Boko’s influence, his international business experience and the challenge of converting Africa’s economic potential into tangible results. He also shares his expectations for the initiative, the importance of global partnerships and his vision for an Africa that creates and retains more value from its resources.

What inspired the creation of the Okavango Circle, who were the key driving forces behind it, and what gaps is the initiative seeking to fill?

The inspiration came from a fundamental question: Why does Africa supply so many of the resources that power the global economy, yet capture so little of the resulting wealth, technology and industrial development?

As a member of the African diaspora, I have long been committed to building stronger commercial relationships between Africa and the United States, connecting African opportunities with international capital, technology and expertise. I believe Africa’s economic transformation and global prosperity can and should reinforce one another.

A defining moment came in 2025, when His Excellency President Duma Boko challenged stakeholders on the sidelines of the 80th United Nations General Assembly to explore mechanisms that would help Africa look beyond the extraction and export of its resources.

That challenge resonated deeply with me. A year later, we returned to the President with the Okavango Circle as a proposed response: a platform designed to bring together African leadership, international partners, investors and technology innovators around a practical agenda for economic transformation.

Our mission is to address the governance of the interconnected forces shaping the global economy: critical minerals, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies and finance. We want to help African countries turn their resource wealth into industries, technological capabilities and sustainable value chains, while creating mutually beneficial commercial partnerships with the wider world.

I am deeply grateful to my fellow co-chairs, Jude Kearney and Ije Agboti-Obatoyinbo, our steering committee and our interim secretariat. Their commitment, expertise and hard work have helped establish the foundation from which we can move towards implementation.

Ultimately, the Okavango Circle is about changing Africa’s position in the global economy—from supplying resources to helping shape, build and benefit from the industries of the future, in partnership with the world.

Why the name Okavango Circle? What significance does it hold, and how does it reflect the initiative’s African identity and global ambitions?

The Okavango Delta is one of the most extraordinary natural treasures on earth. The Okavango River connects Angola, Namibia and Botswana, reminding us that resources, opportunities and shared interests extend beyond national borders.

The Circle represents interconnectedness. Critical minerals, AI, emerging technologies and finance may be distinct sectors, but together they will shape the future of the global economy. Their convergence requires new thinking, effective governance and collaboration among the people and institutions that influence them.

There is also a deeper ambition behind the name. I believe global conversations about Africa’s future should increasingly be shaped and led from Africa itself. The Okavango offers a remarkable African setting from which to bring global leaders together around issues that will affect all our futures.

Just as Davos has become synonymous with the World Economic Forum, we aspire for the Okavango to become synonymous with a new global conversation about how resources, technology, finance and governance can work together to advance sustainable prosperity.

The Okavango Circle is African-housed, globally connected and commercially oriented. We think globally, act locally and believe Africa can help shape a more prosperous future for the world.

How did President Duma Boko become involved with the Okavango Circle, what attracted him to the initiative, and what role will he and the Government of Botswana play going forward?

The story begins with President Duma Boko’s challenge to stakeholders on the sidelines of the 80th UN General Assembly in 2025. He called for practical mechanisms to help Africa move beyond the extraction and removal of its natural resources and capture more of the value those resources can generate.

I regard that intervention as an important catalyst for the Okavango Circle. It gave expression to a challenge that many of us recognized and created an opportunity for stakeholders to come together around a shared ambition.

A year later, we returned to the President with the Okavango Circle as a proposed response. For me, that is an important part of our story. We did not want to return with another set of talking points; we wanted to develop a platform capable of bringing the relevant stakeholders together around a practical agenda.

President Boko’s leadership and vision have helped give the initiative political significance. We also recognize the important perspectives that Honorable Bogolo Kenewendo brings to minerals and industrial development, and Honorable Savannah Maziya brings to the digital and technology dimension.

Going forward, we hope to work constructively with the Government of Botswana and other African partners to develop the institutional foundations, international partnerships and practical programmes needed to advance this mission.

The Okavango Circle is a collective undertaking. Our responsibility is to honour the vision that inspired it by building strong partnerships and delivering meaningful outcomes for Africa and its international partners.

 How would you assess the launch in New York during UNGA 81, the level of international participation, and the key messages and outcomes?

I see the New York launch as an important milestone in bringing the Okavango Circle to the international stage. It gave us an opportunity to introduce our vision and demonstrate the value of bringing political leadership, technology, investment and industry into a single conversation.

The participation of President Duma Boko, Honorable Bogolo Kenewendo and Honorable Savannah Maziya, alongside representatives from government, investment, industry and technology, demonstrated the relevance of the initiative across these interconnected sectors.

I am also grateful to my fellow co-chairs, Jude Kearney and Ije Agboti-Obatoyinbo, our steering committee and our interim secretariat. Their dedication and hard work were instrumental in establishing the foundation for the launch and sustaining our momentum towards implementation.

Three messages stood out.

First, Africa must capture more value from its resources. We must move beyond exporting raw materials and build the industries, capabilities and supply chains that generate lasting economic benefits.

Second, the interconnectedness of minerals, technology and finance must be governed strategically. The countries that shape the rules, mobilize capital and develop technologies will have a significant influence over where economic value is created and retained.

Third, Africa must help shape the global economic agenda. Our ambition is not to exclude international partners, but to engage them on a more strategic and mutually beneficial basis—one that recognizes Africa as a substantive commercial partner.

The launch was a shared achievement and an important foundation. But it was not an end in itself. The real test is whether we can translate that momentum into practical partnerships, investment opportunities, stronger institutions and measurable results.

New York helped introduce our vision to the world. Our responsibility now is to demonstrate that an African-housed global platform can turn that vision into commercial partnerships and sustainable prosperity.

The Okavango Circle focuses on the convergence of critical minerals, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies and finance. What does this mean in practical terms, and what distinguishes your approach from existing global platforms?

At the heart of the Okavango Circle is a fundamental belief: Africa must not only participate in the global economic future; it must help architect it.

Critical minerals, AI, emerging technologies and finance are often addressed as separate sectors. Yet they are deeply interconnected forces that will determine how industries evolve, where investment flows, who controls the technologies of the future and where economic value is created and retained.

Our mission is not simply to bring these sectors together for discussion. It is to address the governance of their interconnectedness: the policies, institutions, investment frameworks and international partnerships needed to ensure that their convergence creates sustainable economic opportunities for Africa and the wider world.

Consider a country with significant lithium or copper deposits. The question is not simply how to extract and export those minerals. It is how to connect those resources with investment in processing and manufacturing, AI-driven innovation, technology development, skilled employment and local businesses. It is also how to shape the governance arrangements that allow these activities to develop into competitive industries and sustainable value chains.

That is where I believe the Okavango Circle can make a distinctive contribution.

Many international initiatives do important work in minerals, technology, finance and economic development. Our ambition is to complement these efforts by focusing on how these sectors interact, how their convergence is governed and how the resulting opportunities can advance Africa’s long-term economic interests.

We want African countries to be co-architects of the policies, partnerships and commercial arrangements that shape these interconnected forces—not simply participants in discussions or recipients of decisions made elsewhere.

But our vision is not inward-looking. As a member of the African diaspora, I have long believed in building stronger commercial relationships between Africa and the United States, and connecting Africa with the wider global economy. Africa’s prosperity creates opportunities for international partners through trade, investment, technology, new markets and shared economic growth.

This is why we describe the Okavango Circle as an African-housed global convening platform. We seek to engage the right international partners to advance sustainable global prosperity, with a particular emphasis on sustainable economic growth in Africa.

Our proposed Technology Convergence Governance Institute will support this ambition through research, policy development and practical partnerships designed to translate strategic thinking into implementation.

Ultimately, our distinction lies in bringing together governance, African leadership and international commercial cooperation.

We are not simply convening a conversation about four sectors. We are seeking to help shape how their convergence is governed, how its opportunities are shared and how Africa can become a co-architect of the global economic future.

Our guiding philosophy is simple: we think globally, act locally and build partnerships that enable Africa and its international partners to prosper together.

 How can the Okavango Circle help African countries move beyond raw mineral exports to attract investment, develop industries, strengthen technological capabilities and create lasting economic value?

The starting point is that mineral wealth does not automatically translate into prosperity. Value comes from the industries, technologies, infrastructure, skills and institutions we build around those resources.

The Okavango Circle seeks to help African countries approach this as an integrated economic and commercial strategy.

First, we want to broaden investment beyond extraction to include processing, refining, advanced materials, manufacturing and related services.

Second, we want to connect mineral development with AI and emerging technologies, while ensuring that African countries build their own technical expertise, research capabilities and technology businesses.

Third, we want to connect resource development to industrial policy so that African businesses can participate in supply chains, provide engineering and technical services, manufacture components and create skilled employment.

Fourth, we want to help bring governments, investors, development finance institutions and international commercial partners together to structure viable projects, mobilize capital and address financing and infrastructure barriers. Regional cooperation will also be important where countries can achieve greater scale by working together.

Finally, we must strengthen governance arrangements that underpin responsible investment, technology transfer, local value creation and sustainable economic growth.

Not every country needs to develop every stage of every value chain. The objective is to identify commercially viable opportunities that reflect each country’s resources, capabilities and market access, while creating opportunities for regional integration.

My experience in international finance and transaction development has taught me that bringing the right people together is only the beginning. Projects must be structured, financing must be aligned, and partnerships must have a clear commercial and economic purpose.

The Okavango Circle can help connect these elements through an integrated approach to governance, policy and international commercial cooperation.

Our ambition is to help transform Africa’s resource wealth into productive industries, stronger technological capabilities and competitive economies—creating value for African countries while building mutually beneficial commercial relationships with the United States and the wider world.

 What are the immediate priorities following the launch, what role will the Technology Convergence Governance Institute play, and when can stakeholders expect the first major activities in Africa?

Our immediate priority is to translate the vision behind the Okavango Circle into a focused programme of work. That means developing the right institutional foundations, engaging African and international partners, identifying priority opportunities and establishing a practical pathway from dialogue to implementation.

The proposed Technology Convergence Governance Institute will be central to this effort. Its intended role is to develop the research, policy frameworks and governance approaches needed to understand and manage the convergence of critical minerals, AI, emerging technologies and finance in Africa’s long-term interests.

But we do not want research and policy to exist in isolation. We want the Institute to help connect policy with commercial opportunities, investment structures and partnerships that can advance industrial development and technological capability.

Our activities in Africa should be grounded in the priorities of participating countries and developed with governments, businesses, universities, investors and other relevant institutions. We also want international partners to be part of this process, bringing capital, expertise, technology and market access into mutually beneficial collaborations.

We will communicate specific programmes and dates as they are confirmed with our partners. Our priority is to ensure that the first major activities establish a credible foundation for sustained engagement and measurable progress.

This is a collective effort, and I am grateful to my fellow co-chairs, steering committee and interim secretariat for helping build the foundation for the work ahead.

The objective is to build an African-housed platform with global reach—one that connects governance, research and commercial partnerships to opportunities that create lasting economic value.

What are your benchmarks for success over the next three to five years, and how will you ensure the Okavango Circle delivers measurable results rather than becoming another international talking shop?

For me, success will not be measured by the number of meetings we convene or declarations we issue. It will be measured by what changes on the ground.

Over the next three to five years, we want to establish clear benchmarks across five areas: investment mobilized, industries developed, technologies adopted, partnerships implemented and lasting economic value created.

Our proposed targets include developing a pipeline of 10–15 investment-ready projects and helping at least five reach financial close within five years. We also aim to support at least three processing, refining or manufacturing projects reaching construction or operation, and advance at least five industry-linked technology pilots towards practical use.

These are proposed targets that must be validated against our resources, project pipeline and participating countries’ priorities before becoming formal commitments. We also intend to measure local procurement, skilled employment, technology transfer and the economic value retained within African economies.

Our approach will be phased. The first year will focus on establishing priorities, baselines, responsibilities and the project pipeline. Years two and three will concentrate on advancing projects, financing and technology partnerships. By years four and five, we want to demonstrate increasingly tangible outcomes in investment, industrial development and technological capability.

We will pursue accountability through defined responsibilities, measurable milestones, regular performance reviews and transparent reporting. We must distinguish between announcements and actual delivery, and be prepared to adjust our approach when results fall short.

But I would add another measure of success: whether we help improve the way these four interconnected sectors are governed, so that African countries have a stronger voice in shaping the investment frameworks, technological partnerships and commercial relationships that influence their economic future.

We do not intend to duplicate existing institutions. Our role is to connect the right expertise, capital and partners around opportunities that benefit from a more integrated approach.

I am encouraged by the commitment of our co-chairs, steering committee and interim secretariat, and by the partnerships we seek to build with African and international stakeholders. Delivering on our ambition will require discipline, collaboration and a willingness to be accountable for results.

We will judge ourselves by the investment deployed, the industries developed, the technologies adopted, the partnerships that deliver and the economic opportunities created. Our ambition is to help Africa become a co-architect of the global economic future—not simply a participant in it.

Beyond the Okavango Circle, you lead Rimsom Global. What are the company’s core activities, geographical footprint and major achievements, and how has your business experience shaped this initiative?

Rimsom Global is a strategic finance and transaction development platform focused on turning high-potential opportunities into bankable investments across emerging markets.

We work with governments, businesses, development institutions, project sponsors, investors and financial partners to originate, structure, finance and advance transformational projects. Our work spans infrastructure, energy, transportation, critical minerals, manufacturing, healthcare, agriculture, the digital economy, AI and industrial development.

Our approach is focused on execution. We seek to remain engaged throughout the transaction lifecycle—from identifying opportunities and preparing projects for investment to structuring capital, mobilizing financing and supporting implementation.

Drawing on more than three decades of international experience in trade policy, export finance, infrastructure, investment promotion and global business development, I have seen both the enormous opportunities available to emerging economies and the challenges they face in turning national priorities into investable projects.

As a member of the African diaspora, I have been particularly committed to strengthening commercial relationships between Africa and the United States. I believe well-structured partnerships can help African countries develop productive industries while creating meaningful opportunities for American businesses and international investors.

That experience has reinforced my conviction that promising ideas need more than capital alone. They require sound governance, technology, commercial expertise and partnerships aligned around a clear economic purpose.

The Okavango Circle builds on that understanding, taking the conversation beyond individual transactions to the governance of the interconnected forces shaping the global economy.

I have been fortunate to work alongside talented colleagues and partners throughout my career, and the Okavango Circle reflects that same belief in collective expertise and shared purpose.

Ultimately, both Rimsom Global and the Okavango Circle are driven by a common principle: connect the right people, capital, technology and opportunities to create measurable and lasting economic value.

What is your long-term vision for the Okavango Circle, what message do you have for potential African and international partners, and what legacy would you like the initiative to leave?

My long-term vision is to establish the Okavango Circle as a globally respected, African-housed platform that helps shape the governance of the interconnected forces driving the global economy—and translates that work into sustainable economic growth for Africa and shared prosperity with the world.

The initiative was inspired in part by President Duma Boko’s challenge to stakeholders in 2025 to help Africa look beyond the extraction and export of its resources. I see the Circle as a collective effort to respond to that challenge by connecting African priorities with international capital, technology, expertise and commercial partnerships.

My message to African partners is that we must approach this moment with ambition, strategic clarity and a stronger sense of collective purpose. We must look beyond the immediate revenues from resource extraction and focus on building industries, technological capabilities and institutions that will sustain prosperity for generations.

To our international partners, my message is equally clear: Africa is not simply a source of resources or an emerging market. It is a substantive commercial partner and must have a meaningful role in shaping the industries and economic systems of the future. We welcome partners prepared to build long-term relationships based on responsible investment, technology transfer, local value creation and mutual benefit.

I am grateful to President Boko for the leadership and vision that helped bring this challenge into focus, and to Honorable Bogolo Kenewendo and Honorable Savannah Maziya for the important perspectives they bring. I also want to recognize my fellow co-chairs, Jude Kearney and Ije Agboti-Obatoyinbo, our steering committee and our interim secretariat. Their commitment has been fundamental to establishing the foundation for this initiative and sustaining our determination to move towards implementation.

The Okavango Circle is a collective undertaking, and its success will depend on the strength of these relationships and our shared determination to turn ambition into results.

The legacy I hope we leave is one in which Africa is better positioned to shape the global economic agenda, build competitive industries, strengthen technological capabilities and retain more of the value generated by its resources.

I want that legacy to be measured in investments deployed, industries established, African businesses strengthened, young people equipped with skills, technologies adopted and quality jobs created. I also want it reflected in stronger commercial relationships between Africa, the United States and the wider international community.

Ultimately, I want the Okavango Circle to be remembered not simply for the conversations it convened, but for the partnerships it made possible, the governance frameworks it helped advance and the industries and opportunities it helped create.

My hope is that we will look back and see that, through collective leadership and meaningful international partnerships, we helped Africa become a co-architect of the global economic future—and demonstrated that sustainable African growth and sustainable global prosperity are mutually reinforcing goals.

*Culled from November Edition of PAV Magazine
